taxonomyNote: NatureServe gives 'Red-bellied Snake' as its standard name and questions the validity of the subspecies pahasapae; Missouri Department of Conservation says subspecies are no longer recognised.
fieldMarks: Very small snake, 20-41 cm; gray, brown or reddish-brown, often with four faint dark stripes and/or a pale or red-orange mid-dorsal stripe.
Belly usually bright red, orange or pink (rarely yellow, gray or black).
Three light spots around the neck (top and each side) sometimes fuse into a collar; white chin and throat, keeled scales (15 rows), divided anal plate.
behavior: Secretive, hiding under bark, logs, rocks and leaf litter; diurnal but nocturnal in hot or dry weather, more active after rain.
Specialist feeder on slugs and snails, also earthworms and insect larvae; hibernates in ant mounds, foundations and animal burrows.
Active April to October/November in the north and year-round in the south; migrates between floodplain and hillside overwintering sites.
habitat: Mostly moist deciduous and mixed forests, bog and swamp edges and adjacent meadows with abundant ground cover; often near buildings.
range: Eastern North America: United States from eastern North Dakota and Wyoming (Black Hills) to the Atlantic and Gulf; in Canada Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island (NatureServe also shows Newfoundland as an exotic record).

lookalikes.name: Copperhead (young)
lookalikes.howToTell: Copperheads are stout-bodied with hourglass markings, vertical pupils and a pit between nostril and eye (Missouri Department of Conservation).

lookalikes.name: Dekay's brownsnake
lookalikes.howToTell: Brownsnake has a tan back stripe flanked by two rows of small dark spots and a cream, yellow or pink belly, whereas the red-bellied snake typically has a red or orange belly and three light nape spots (Missouri Department of Conservation).
